A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. derivations.claim: Let $\alpha=D\cap A$ and $\beta=D\cap\partial M$. Essentiality of the arc $\alpha$ in the annulus means that it joins the two distinct boundary circles of $A$. Each circle of $\partial A$ is essential on its boundary torus: if one bounded a disk in that torus, pushing the disk slightly into a boundary collar would give a compressing disk for $A$.

On a boundary torus containing one circle of $\partial A$, its complement is an annulus; if it contains both parallel circles, the complement is two annuli. Thus $\beta$ lies in an annular component $A_0$ of the torus cut along $\partial A$. If $\beta$ were boundary-parallel in $A_0$, adjoining the disk it cuts off to $D$ would give a compressing disk for $A$. Hence $\beta$ spans $A_0$. Its endpoints therefore lie on distinct circles of $\partial A$.

The annulus $A$ and the spanning annulus in $\partial M$ form an embedded torus $S$. The curve $\alpha\cup\beta$ crosses the core of $A$ once modulo $2$, so it is nontrivial in $H_1(S;\mathbb Z_2)$ and cannot bound a disk. Thus $D$ compresses $S$ to an embedded sphere.

Irreducibility gives a $3$-ball bounded by the compressed sphere. Reversing the compression attaches one $1$-handle to that ball, producing a solid torus bounded by $S$. In its boundary, $A$ and the annulus in $\partial M$ are complementary annuli. A collar of the latter in this solid torus is a product between the two annuli; rounding the disk-surgery corner gives a product $A\times[0,1]$ in $M$ with one end in $\partial M$. Therefore $A$ is boundary-parallel.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and
the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of
closed faces is a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary
incompatible boundary data is asserted.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable piecewise linear three-manifold with a given finite compatible manifold triangulation and with boundary a subcomplex. Let $F\subset\partial M$ be a connected compact piecewise linear subsurface and $N\trianglelefteq\pi_1(F)$ a normal subgroup. Suppose there is a continuous map $f:(D^2,\partial D^2)\to(M,F)$ whose boundary lies in the relative interior of $F$ and has class outside $N$. Then there is a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$, with boundary in the relative interior of $F$, whose boundary class is outside $N$.

In particular, if a connected boundary component has noninjective induced fundamental-group map into $M$, it contains an essential simple closed curve bounding a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$. Boundary classes outside $N$ are understood up to conjugation by a basepath in $F$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Every element of $G\ast_KH$ has a unique normal form $s_1\cdots s_nk$ relative to fixed transversals. A normal word of positive length is nonidentity. The represented group and these conclusions are independent of the chosen transversals.

derivations.claim: Choose a meridian disk $D_0$ and put $F$ transverse to it. Every circle of $F\cap D_0$ bounds a disk in $D_0$. An essential circle gives a compressing disk for $F$; for an inessential circle, an innermost disk in $D_0$ and the disk it bounds in $F$ form a sphere. Since the standard solid torus is embedded in $S^3$ and its complement is connected, [F5] implies this sphere bounds a ball in $V$. Isotopy across that ball removes the circle. Repeating this finite reduction leaves only arcs.

An outermost arc of $F\cap D_0$ cuts off a boundary-compressing disk. Boundary-incompressibility implies that its arc on $F$ cuts off a disk in $F$. The other boundary arc must then have both endpoints on the same side of the corresponding meridian arc in $\partial V$. But an arc transverse to the meridian circles runs monotonically through them, so it cannot have both endpoints on that same side. Thus the intersection arcs can be removed, and $F$ is isotoped disjoint from $D_0$.

Cutting $V$ along $D_0$ gives a ball. Every boundary circle of $F$ on the ball's boundary sphere bounds a disk there; choose an innermost one. If $F$ were not a disk, that pushed-in disk would have essential boundary on $F$ and would compress it. Therefore $F$ is a disk, and regluing $D_0$ shows that its boundary is a meridian of $V$.

Two meridian disks with the same boundary cut the solid torus to disks in a ball with the same boundary. The disk isotopy in the ball, fixed on that boundary, descends after regluing $D_0$ to an isotopy of the meridian disks relative to their boundary.

Let $T\subset\operatorname{int}V$ be a two-sided embedded torus. If $T$ did not separate $V$, a path in the connected complement joining its two local sides, closed by a short transverse arc, would give a loop meeting $T$ once modulo $2$. This contradicts $H_2(V;\mathbb Z_2)=0$, since mod-two intersection with a closed surface depends only on its homology class. Hence $T$ separates $V$ into compact orientable pieces $W_1,W_2$.

Give $V,W_1,W_2$ finite compatible triangulations by [F2]. Collar neighbourhoods of $W_1,W_2$ form an open cover with overlap retracting to $T$. If both inclusions $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1(W_i)$ were injective, [F4] and van Kampen would identify $\pi_1(V)$ with the amalgamated product $\pi_1(W_1)*_{\pi_1(T)}\pi_1(W_2)$, and the normal form theorem would embed $\pi_1(T)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ in $\pi_1(V)\cong\mathbb Z$. Since no injective homomorphism $\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb Z$ exists, one side inclusion has nontrivial kernel.

Apply [F3] to that side with boundary subsurface the copy of $T$. It is compact, orientable, and finitely triangulated, and the inclusion kernel is nontrivial. The Loop Theorem gives a properly embedded disk whose boundary is essential on $T$ and whose interior misses $T$; this is a compressing disk for $T$ in $V$.

derivations.claim: Use the finite triangulation supplied in the Statement. Put the torus family in general position with its strata in increasing dimension: first make it disjoint from vertices, then transverse to open edges, then transverse to open triangular faces, keeping fixed collars of strata already treated. At each stage only finitely many embedded strata occur. By [F1], each bad-parameter set is null, so the complement of their finite union is dense in every small parameter ball; choose a perturbation there. Choose each perturbation small enough in $C^1$ to preserve the previously achieved transverse intersections and their fixed collars. This yields one finite general position for the whole triangulation.

Simplify each intersection with a tetrahedron by innermost-circle surgery: incompressibility supplies a disk in the torus with the surgery boundary, and irreducibility makes the resulting sphere bound a ball, so pushing across that ball realizes the surgery by isotopy. This removes all non-disk components in tetrahedra and all circular components in faces. Next remove every arc in a triangular face whose endpoints lie on the same edge, using an outermost such arc and an isotopy across the disk it cuts off. Thus each face is cut by disjoint arcs joining distinct edges. At most four complementary regions in a triangular face fail to be rectangles: the three regions incident to its vertices and at most one central region.

A cut component meeting every triangular face only in rectangular strips has a local interval direction across each tetrahedron. The strip directions agree on common faces, so they form an interval-bundle structure on that component. A trivial bundle over a torus would be a forbidden $T^2\times[0,1]$ component. Each remaining such component is a regular neighbourhood of a closed one-sided surface; write these pairwise disjoint surfaces as $Q_1,\ldots,Q_m$.

Since $M$ is connected, use a spanning tree in the dual graph of the torus cuts and order the non-tree edges first. The corresponding first $k$ tori are nonseparating when successively cut; each remaining tree-edge torus separates its current component. The dual graph of those remaining pieces and separating tori is therefore a tree. In each rectangular-only piece, the one-sided core $Q_j$ has connected complement: its twisted interval-bundle neighbourhood minus the core retracts to the connected double-cover boundary of that neighbourhood. Removing all $Q_j$ therefore keeps each such piece connected, and the tree of pieces remains connected when its separating torus faces are identified. Thus the complement of the first $k$ tori and all $Q_j$ is connected. Their mod-two homology classes are linearly independent: a nonempty relation would make a nonempty subcollection the boundary of a $3$-chain, and such a boundary disconnects its complement, contrary to connectedness. Therefore $k+m\le\beta$.

If $n=|\mathcal T|$, the first $k$ cuts leave the manifold connected and each remaining cut adds one component, so cutting along $\mathcal T$ gives $n-k+1$ components. At most $m$ are the nontrivial interval-bundle neighbourhoods from step 2.1. Every other component meets a nonrectangular region in some triangular face from step 1.2, and distinct components use distinct regions. There are at most $4t$ such regions, so $n-k+1\le m+4t$.

Combining $k+m\le\beta$ with $n-k+1\le m+4t$ gives $n+1\le k+m+4t\le\beta+4t$. Hence $n\le4t+\beta-1$. At every stage of the stated process this same bound applies to the accumulated torus family, so no process satisfying the no-product condition can make more than that many cuts.

For a based Serre fibration $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ with fiber $F=p^{-1}(b_0)$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to\pi_n(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_n(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_n(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_{n-1}(F)\to\cdots\to\pi_1(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_0(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_0(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_0(B)$$
is exact wherever there is an incoming and outgoing arrow. Basepoints are $e_0,b_0$ as appropriate. Exactness means incoming image equals the inverse image of the distinguished element. Arrows are homomorphisms where both group structures are defined; the component terms are pointed sets. The last arrow is onto precisely when $p(E)$ meets every path component of $B$.

There is a right action of $\pi_1(B,b_0)$ on $\pi_0(F)$: $[e]\cdot[\gamma]$ is the endpoint component of a lift of $\gamma$ starting at $e$, with loop products traversed left-to-right. Its orbits are precisely the fibers of $i_*:\pi_0(F)\to\pi_0(E)$, and the stabilizer of $[e_0]$ is $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$. Our boundary convention gives $\partial_p[\gamma]=[e_0]\cdot[\gamma]^{-1}$. These assertions require no AC.

The fundamental group of a pair of pants is free on two generators $a,b$, and its three boundary loops represent $a$, $b$, and $(ab)^{-1}$, each of infinite order. The once-punctured Möbius band has free generators $x,c_1$ and boundary loops represented by $c_1$ and $c_1^{-1}x^{-2}$; both are nontrivial cyclically reduced words and have infinite order in the free group. Thus every boundary circle of $B$ injects on fundamental groups.

The restriction $T\to\partial B$ is a circle bundle over a circle, hence induces a surjection $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1(\partial B)$. If $g\in\pi_1(T)$ maps trivially to $\pi_1(N)$, its projection is a power of the corresponding boundary loop and is trivial in $\pi_1(B)$; step 1.2 forces that power to be zero. Therefore $g$ lies in the fiber subgroup, whose inclusion into $\pi_1(N)$ is injective by step 1.1, so $g=1$. This proves that $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1(N)$ is injective.

Their inverse images are disjoint vertical annuli $A_1,\ldots,A_r$, and cutting $M_0$ along them gives a solid torus $W$.

Use [F4] to put $F$ transverse to these annuli and to the chosen fiber cores, and minimize the number of intersection components. An inessential circle of $F\cap A_j$ can be removed by an innermost-disk isotopy: if it is essential in $F$ it gives a compression, and otherwise the disk on $F$ together with the disk on $A_j$ bounds a sphere, which bounds a ball in $M$ by irreducibility. Remove outermost arcs with both endpoints on the same boundary component of $A_j$; if their endpoints lie on an original boundary component, they give a boundary compression of $F$, and if they lie on a deleted fiber-neighbourhood boundary, isotopy across the outermost disk lowers the number of intersections with the corresponding core fiber. If a component of $F_1$ had a compressing disk, its boundary is nullhomotopic in $F$ by incompressibility of $F$; [F5] then bounds the resulting sphere by a ball, and pushing across that ball removes intersection curves, contradicting minimality. Every boundary circle of $F_1$ is vertical or horizontal on $\partial W$, hence essential. Each component with boundary is incompressible. By [F3] it is boundary-incompressible or a boundary-parallel annulus; a boundary-incompressible component is not boundary-parallel, since a boundary-parallel annulus has a boundary compression and a boundary-parallel disk has nullhomotopic boundary. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $V=S^1\times D^2$ be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core $S^1\times\{0\}$. A **pattern** is a smooth oriented knot $P$ contained in the interior of $V$, together with a chosen closed tubular neighbourhood $N(P)$ contained in the interior of $V$. Its **winding number** $w(P)$ is the integer by which the homology class $[P]$ maps to $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ under the isomorphism that sends the oriented core to $1$. The **pattern exterior** is $X_P=V\setminus\operatorname{int}N(P)$; its **outer torus** is $\partial V$ and its **inner torus** is $\partial N(P)$. A **companion** is a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ with a specified orientation-preserving tubular embedding $e:V\to S^3$ that sends the core to $K$ and identifies the solid-torus meridian and product longitude with the positive meridian and preferred longitude of $K$. The **satellite knot** $P(K)$ is $e(P)$, with chosen exterior $E_{P(K)}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}e(N(P))$; the image $e(\partial V)$ is its **companion torus**. The outer torus is **incompressible** when it bounds no properly embedded disk in $X_P$ with essential boundary on $\partial V$. It is **product-parallel** to the inner torus when $X_P$ is a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with those tori as its ends. Let $T_c=e(\partial V)\subset E_{P(K)}$ be the companion torus. Then $T_c$ is incompressible and is not boundary-parallel in $E_{P(K)}$; hence it is essential.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. Assume full AC. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen compact exterior $E_K$. There exists a finite inclusion-minimal collection $\mathcal T$ of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori in the interior of $E_K$ such that every component of $E_K$ cut along $\mathcal T$ is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. Any two such inclusion-minimal collections are ambient isotopic in $E_K$. Atoroidal pieces in this statement are not asserted to be hyperbolic.

Let $p,q$ be coprime nonzero integers, let $K=T(p,q)$ be the oriented primitive slope curve in the standard Heegaard torus, and let $\rho_t(z_1,z_2)=(e^{2\pi i p t}z_1,e^{2\pi i q t}z_2)$ be the weighted circle action on the unit $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$. Let $x$ and $y$ be based generators of the fundamental groups of the two solid-torus pieces obtained by cutting $E_K$ along the annulus left on the Heegaard torus, oriented so that the annulus core maps to $x^p$ and $y^q$. $$\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle.$$

The core $S^1\times\{0\}$ has stabilizer of order $2$, while generic points have trivial stabilizer. Removing a tube about the regular orbit $P_{2,1}$ therefore gives a Seifert fibration of $X_{P_{2,1}}$ over an annulus with one exceptional point of multiplicity $2$. On the outer torus its regular-fiber slope is $2\lambda_V+\mu_V$.

Remove a small neighborhood of the exceptional point from the annulus base. The remaining pair of pants has fundamental group freely generated by a loop $a$ around the outer boundary and a loop $c$ around the removed cone point; its third boundary loop is $(ac)^{-1}$. The circle bundle over this pair of pants has a section: it retracts to a graph, and a section over that graph is obtained by choosing one point in the fiber at the vertex and extending over each edge. Thus its group has generators $a,c,h$, with $h$ the fiber and $[a,h]=[c,h]=1$. The order-two local model $(z,w)\mapsto(-z,-w)$ around the exceptional core identifies the filled meridian with $c^2h$ after replacing $c$ by $ch^k$ if necessary: one circuit of the cone-point boundary lifts from $(z,w)$ to $(-z,-w)$, so two circuits equal one inverse fiber turn, and the twisting coefficient is odd. Filling that neighborhood kills this meridian. By [F3],
$$
\pi_1(X_{P_{2,1}})=\langle a,c,h\mid [a,h]=[c,h]=1,\ c^2h=1\rangle.
$$
Its quotient by $\langle h\rangle$ is $\mathbb Z*C_2$, which is nonabelian by reduced normal forms [F4]; hence $X_{P_{2,1}}$ is not $T^2\times I$. Its outer boundary subgroup is generated by $a,h$. The abelianization is free on $[a],[c]$ with $[h]=-2[c]$, so $a^m h^n=1$ implies $m=0$ and $n=0$. Thus the outer torus group injects into $\pi_1(X_{P_{2,1}})$ and has no compressing disk.

Its quotient by $\langle h_K\rangle$ is $C_2*C_3$, nonabelian by [F4], and $h_K$ is infinite because its abelianization is $6$ times the generator of $H_1(E_K)\cong\mathbb Z$. The group maps onto $S_3$ by $x\mapsto(12)$ and $y\mapsto(123)$, so it is nonabelian and $K$ is not the unknot, whose exterior group is $\mathbb Z$.

The peripheral formula in [F2] gives $h_K=\lambda_K+6\mu_K$. The companion embedding identifies $(\mu_V,\lambda_V)$ with $(\mu_K,\lambda_K)$. Therefore the two Seifert fibrations on the cut sides induce slopes $2\lambda+\mu$ and $\lambda+6\mu$ on the companion torus. Their determinant in the ordered basis $(\mu,\lambda)$ is $\det\begin{pmatrix}1&6\\2&1\end{pmatrix}=-11$, so the slopes are not parallel.
By [F7], the companion torus $T_c$ is essential. Hence the whole exterior $M=E_{P_{2,1}(K)}$ is not atoroidal. Both pieces cut along $T_c$ are Seifert-fibered by steps 1.1 and 2.1.

Suppose $M$ had a Seifert fibration. It is irreducible by [[lem-knot-exterior-is-irreducible]], so [F6] makes $T_c$ ambient isotopic to a vertical or horizontal torus. Isotopy preserves the homeomorphism types of the cut pieces. In the horizontal case, cutting along $T_c$ gives interval bundles over compact connected surfaces, so each side group is a surface group.

The horizontal case is impossible. The cable group has torsion-free abelianization $\mathbb Z^2$ and contains the nontrivial central element $h$. By [F5], the only compact connected surface groups with torsion-free rank-two abelianization are $\mathbb Z^2$ and the free group of rank two; their centers are the whole group and trivial, respectively. The cable group is nonabelian (its quotient by $h$ is $\mathbb Z*C_2$), so it is neither. The trefoil group has abelianization $\mathbb Z$ and is nonabelian (it maps onto $S_3$), while by [F5] the only compact connected surface groups with torsion-free rank-one abelianization are infinite cyclic groups. Thus neither cut piece can be an interval bundle over a surface.

Conjugation along any loop preserves or reverses a regular fiber, so $g^2$ is central in $\pi_1(M)$. Likewise the trefoil group has center exactly $\langle h_K\rangle$, since $h_K$ is central and infinite and the quotient is $C_2*C_3$, whose center is trivial by reduced-word normal forms. In $\mathbb Z*C_2$, a central word lies in both factor centralizers $\langle a\rangle$ and $\langle c\rangle$; in $C_2*C_3$, it lies in both factor centralizers $C_2$ and $C_3$. Reduced normal forms give these centralizers and each intersection is trivial. Thus in each boundary-torus group the class of $g^2$ is a nonzero power of that side's regular fiber.
